pos: n. (God's eternal, unconditional choice of particular persons to salvation in Christ; the fountain of the ordo salutis)
etymology: Latin electio, a choosing out, from eligere (e- out + legere to pick). Greek eklogē (G1589), selection; eklektos (G1588), chosen. The New Testament word is not a vote among options. It is God taking a people for Himself.
biblical_def: Election is God's eternal, sovereign, and unconditional choice of particular persons to salvation in Christ. Paul locates it before creation: “According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love” (Eph 1:4). The ground is not foreseen faith or works: “that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth” (Rom 9:11). The chain that follows has no broken link: “Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified” (Rom 8:30). Christ says to the disciples, “Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you” (John 15:16). The calling itself is “not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began” (2Ti 1:9). And it is of grace or it is not election: “there is a remnant according to the election of grace” (Rom 11:5). The right question is not why God chose some, but why He chose any. All were dead in sins. The doctrine does not chill evangelism. It guarantees that the gospel will find its people.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines election as the act of choosing, and, in theology, the divine choice by which persons are distinguished as objects of mercy, become subjects of grace, are sanctified and prepared for heaven.
webster_full: ELEC'TION, n. [L. electio.] The act of choosing; choice; the act of selecting one or more from others.
2. The act of choosing a person to fill an office or employment, by any manifestation of preference.
3. Choice; voluntary preference; free will; liberty to act or not. It is at his election to accept or refuse.

6. In theology, divine choice; predetermination of God, by which persons are distinguished as objects of mercy, become subjects of grace, are sanctified and prepared for heaven. There is a remnant according to the election of grace. Romans 11:5.
9. Those who are elected. The election hath obtained it. Romans 11:5.
scriptures: Eph 1:4
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:
Rom 9:11
(For the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth;)
Rom 8:30
Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.
John 15:16

Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you, that ye should go and bring forth fruit, and that your fruit should remain: that whatsoever ye shall ask of the Father in my name, he may give it you.
Who hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began,
corruption_summary: Election is treated as an optional Calvinist extra, and Romans 9 is written to stop that move.
corruption_paragraphs: Popular Christianity avoids the word, then answers the objections Romans 9 already named. It is not fair. It cancels free will. It makes God arbitrary. Paul's reply is not to soften the decree. It is to assert it more plainly, and to ask who thou art that repliest against God. The real offense is that election dethrones the human will as the last court of appeal. A God who offers and waits is easier to market than a God who chooses, calls, and saves. The biblical God does the second, and He is not embarrassed by it.

Two opposite corruptions then appear. One denies election altogether and makes foreseen faith the ground of the choice, which is to put the effect in the place of the cause. The other admits election and then grows cold toward the lost, as if the decree were an excuse to stop preaching. Paul preached to the elect without knowing their names, and he did it as a debtor. The remnant according to the election of grace is not a club. It is a people still being gathered by the ordinary means of the Word.

Assurance follows the chain, not the temperature of the heart on a given morning. Whom He predestinated, them He also called, them He also justified, them He also glorified. The verbs are God's. A man looking at his own stability is looking in the wrong place. The elect cannot be lost because their salvation does not rest in the will that first refused Him.
roots_summary: Greek eklogē (G1589), election; eklektos (G1588), elect; eklegomai (G1586), to choose out; proorizō (G4309), to mark out beforehand.
roots_lines: Greek eklogē (G1589) — election, selection; Romans 9:11, 11:5, 11:7, 1 Thessalonians 1:4.
Greek eklektos (G1588) — elect, chosen; Matthew 24:22, 1 Peter 2:9, 2 Timothy 2:10.
Greek proorizō (G4309) — to predestinate; Romans 8:29-30, Ephesians 1:5, 1:11, Acts 4:28.
usage: “Not of works, but of him that calleth” — the children not yet born.
“Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you” — said to men who thought they had volunteered.
“The election of grace” — if it is of grace, the ground is not in the chosen.

pos: n. (the Reformation doctrine that Scripture, in all things necessary to salvation, is clear enough for the ordinary reader using ordinary means)
etymology: Latin perspicuitas, clearness, from perspicuus, able to be seen through, from perspicere (per- through + specere to look). The Reformers used the word for the Bible, not for a writer's style. God is not a poor communicator.
biblical_def: Perspicuity is the doctrine that the Scriptures, in all things necessary to be known, believed, and observed for salvation, are clear enough that a man does not need a magisterium to reach them. “Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path” (Psa 119:105). Light is given to walk by, not locked in a cabinet. “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130). The simple are not barred. “The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple” (Psa 19:7). Moses had already shut the door on the hidden-word religion: “For this commandment which I command thee this day, it is not hidden from thee, neither is it far off” (Deu 30:11). And Timothy knew the holy scriptures “from a child,” which “are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus” (2Ti 3:15). The doctrine does not say every verse is equally plain on first reading. It says the way of life is not a secret kept from the people of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines perspicuity as clearness to mental vision, easiness to be understood, freedom from obscurity or ambiguity; that quality of writing or language which readily presents to the mind the precise ideas of the author.
webster_full: PERSPICU'ITY, n. [L. perspicuitas, from perspicio.]
1. Transparency; clearness; that quality of a substance which renders objects visible through it. [Little used.]

2. Clearness to mental vision; easiness to be understood; freedom from obscurity or ambiguity; that quality of writing or language which readily presents to the mind of another the precise ideas of the author.
Perspicuity is the first excellence of writing or speaking.
scriptures: NUN. Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
Psa 19:7
The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple.
For this commandment which I command thee this day, it is not hidden from thee, neither is it far off.
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: Rome locked the book behind a court of interpreters, and the modern academy locks it behind credentials. Both say the ordinary reader cannot be trusted with it.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome's historic claim is that Scripture in untrained hands is dangerous, and that the church alone may say what it means. That is still the formal position. It treats the Word as a code and the Magisterium as the decoder, which is to put the church over the text that created the church. The Reformers' answer was not that every ploughboy instantly understands Ezekiel. It was that what a man must know to be saved is so clearly opened in some place of Scripture or other that the unlearned, in a due use of the ordinary means, may attain a sufficient understanding of it. Westminster 1.7 said it because the Bible had already said it.

The academy now runs the same operation from the other side. The text is declared too ancient, too ideological, too linguistically freighted for anyone but a guild to handle. Ordinary reading is called naive. The result is the same gate: an elite between the sheep and the Shepherd's voice. God wrote to be understood. He sent His Spirit to open the understanding. A Bible that only experts may read is not a Bible for the people, and that was never the design.

Perspicuity is also not a license to skip hard work. “Making wise the simple” does not mean the simple need no lamp, no preaching, no comparing of Scripture with Scripture. It means the lamp works. The man who waits for a court to tell him whether John 3:16 may be believed has already denied the doctrine.
roots_summary: Hebrew or (H216), light; pethi (H6612), the simple; Greek phōs (G5457), light; haplous related simplicity of eye; graphē (G1124), scripture.
roots_lines: Hebrew or (H216) — light; Psalm 119:105, 119:130, of the Word as what makes plain.
Hebrew pethi (H6612) — the simple; Psalm 19:7, 119:130 — the Word makes them wise.
Greek hiera grammata (G2413, G1121) — the holy scriptures; 2 Timothy 3:15, able to make wise unto salvation.
usage: “A lamp unto my feet” — given to walk by, not locked in a cabinet.
“It giveth understanding unto the simple” — the simple are not barred.
“It is not hidden from thee, neither is it far off” — Moses against the hidden-word religion.

pos: n. phrase (the legal, living, and covenantal bond by which the believer is in Christ and Christ in the believer; the hinge of salvation)
etymology: Latin unio, oneness, from unus, one. The old theological name is unio cum Christo. Calvin called it the principal hinge on which religion turns. Paul's ordinary phrase is en Christō, in Christ, used of the believer more than a hundred times.
biblical_def: Union with Christ is the real bond by which a believer is joined to Jesus Christ and shares in what He is and has done. It is not a mood. It is not a metaphor for feeling near God. Christ commands it as a living connection: “Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me” (John 15:4). He adds the sentence that ends self-help: “for without me ye can do nothing” (John 15:5). Paul states the same union as a death and a life: “I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me” (Gal 2:20). Baptism names the legal side: “we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life” (Rom 6:4). And the intimacy is not less than marriage's: “he that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit” (1Co 6:17). Every spiritual blessing is located there: “who hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ” (Eph 1:3). Justification, adoption, sanctification, and glory do not arrive as loose gifts. They come with the Person.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines union as the act of joining two or more things into one, and as concord, agreement and conjunction of mind, will, affections or interest; also the junction of spirit and matter, as the union of soul and body.
webster_full: U'NION, n. [L. unio, to unite, from unus, one.]
1. The act of joining two or more things into one, and thus forming a compound body or a mixture; or the junction or coalition of things thus united.
2. Concord; agreement and conjunction of mind, will, affections or interest. Happy is the family where perfect union subsists between all its members.
3. The junction or united existence of spirit and matter; as the union of soul and body.
Union differs from connection, as it implies the bodies to be in contact, without an intervening body.
scriptures: John 15:4
Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me.
John 15:5
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
Gal 2:20

I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.
Rom 6:4
Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.
But he that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit.
corruption_summary: Union with Christ is turned into either a dissolving of the person into God, or a vague sense of closeness that asks nothing of the cross.
corruption_paragraphs: One distortion reads the vine as absorption. The branch is said to lose itself in the divine whole, which is the old Gnostic and Eastern move, not Paul's. The man who says “yet not I, but Christ liveth in me” is still a man. He still lives in the flesh by the faith of the Son of God. Union is intimate. It is not identity. We do not become Christ, and we are not merged into the divine essence. The Creator-creature line holds even when the Spirit indwells.

The other distortion is softer and more common. “In Christ” is used as a slogan for a preferred religious feeling, a private closeness that can be taken up or laid down with the week. Paul's en Christō is objective. It is the location of election, redemption, and inheritance in Ephesians 1. A man is in Christ or he is not. The branch that does not abide is not a branch having a dry season. It is cut off. Feelings follow union. They do not create it.

Federal union is the legal spine. We were in Adam, and his disobedience was ours; we are in Christ, and His death and resurrection are ours (Rom 6). That is why baptism is into His death, and why there is no receiving of forgiveness while remaining unconnected to the Person who accomplished it. The benefits are not separable from Him.
roots_summary: Greek en Christō, in Christ; menō (G3306), to abide; sustauroō (G4957), to crucify with; kollaō (G2853), to join.
roots_lines: Greek en Christō (G1722, G5547) — in Christ; Ephesians 1:3, Romans 8:1, 2 Corinthians 5:17.
Greek menō (G3306) — abide; John 15:4-7, the vine's verb.
Greek kollaō (G2853) — to join, glue; 1 Corinthians 6:17, joined unto the Lord.
usage: “Without me ye can do nothing” — not less, not some things.
“Yet not I, but Christ liveth in me” — the man is still there; the life is not his old one.
“Joined unto the Lord is one spirit” — closer than a contract.

pos: n. (the classical attribute: God is not composed of parts; His being and His attributes are not assembled pieces)
etymology: Latin simplicitas, singleness, from simplex, uncompounded. The 1689 Confession says God is “a most pure spirit, invisible, without body, parts, or passions.” Simplicity is that line: no parts.
biblical_def: Divine simplicity teaches that God is not put together. He does not have love as a detachable part, holiness as another, will as a third. He is what He is, wholly. Scripture does not say God possesses love as a quality He might lay down. It says “God is love” (1Jn 4:8). It says “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all” (1Jn 1:5). It says “God is a Spirit” (John 4:24). The name He gives Moses is the same claim in the first person: “I AM THAT I AM” (Exo 3:14). And Israel's creed is undivided being: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD” (Deu 6:4). If God were composed of parts, something would be prior to God — the cause of the composition. But God is uncaused. He does not become more just by cooling His mercy, or more merciful by muting His justice. The cross is not two attributes negotiating. It is one God, doing one work, in which justice and mercy are not rivals.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines simplicity as singleness, the state of being unmixed or uncompounded; also plainness, freedom from subtilty or abstruseness, as the simplicity of scriptural doctrines or truth.
webster_full: SIMPLIC'ITY, n. [L. simplicitas.]
1. Singleness; the state of being unmixed or uncompounded; as the simplicity of metals or of earths.
2. The state of being not complex, or of consisting of few parts; as the simplicity of a machine.
3. Artlessness of mind; freedom from a propensity to cunning or stratagem; freedom from duplicity; sincerity.
5. Plainness; freedom from subtilty or abstruseness; as the simplicity of scriptural doctrines or truth.
scriptures: He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love.
This then is the message which we have heard of him, and declare unto you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.
Exo 3:14
And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you.
Deu 6:4
Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD:
John 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
corruption_summary: God is imagined as a committee of attributes, so that love can be played against holiness, and Open Theism can give Him parts that change.
corruption_paragraphs: The popular move is to pick one attribute, usually love, and treat the rest as problems to be managed. A God who “is love” is then forbidden to judge, as if 1 John 4:8 cancelled 1 John 1:5. Simplicity forbids the move. The same God who is love is light, and in Him is no darkness at all. Mercy and justice are not two departments that take turns. They are two names we give, from our side, to the one undivided God as He deals with sinners. The cross is where a man sees both without remainder.

Open Theism and some social-Trinitarian schemes reject simplicity because they want a God who can acquire new states, take risks, and be a genuine partner in the world's process. That is not the I AM of Exodus 3. A God with parts can be improved. The God of Scripture cannot, and that is good news. His love will not cool. His promise will not be revised by a new mood in the Godhead.

The Confession's “without body, parts, or passions” is not a denial that God is living, willing, and personal. It is the denial that He is a composite who might come apart. He is one LORD. The Trinity is not three parts of God. It is three Persons who are the one simple God. Simplicity and Trinity are not rivals. They are the two rails that keep the doctrine from collapsing into unitarianism on one side and tritheism on the other.
roots_summary: Hebrew echad (H259), one; ehyeh (H1961), I AM; Greek theos agapē estin, God is love; pneuma ho theos, God is spirit.
roots_lines: Hebrew ehyeh asher ehyeh (H1961) — I AM THAT I AM; Exodus 3:14, self-existence without composition.
Hebrew YHWH echad (H3068, H259) — the LORD is one; Deuteronomy 6:4.
Greek ho theos agapē estin (G26) — God is love; 1 John 4:8, 4:16 — identity, not a detachable property.
usage: “God is love” — not has love in a drawer He might shut.
“I AM THAT I AM” — no parts, no becoming, no prior cause.
“The LORD our God is one LORD” — undivided, not a committee of attributes.

pos: n. (the Spirit-enabled putting to death of sin in the believer; not the managing of it)
etymology: Latin mortificare, to put to death, from mors, death, + facere, to make. The Authorized Version's verb is mortify. Owen's title still tells the truth: the mortification of sin in believers.
biblical_def: Mortification is the believer's ongoing work of putting sin to death by the Spirit. It is commanded, not offered as a temperament: “For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live” (Rom 8:13). The same order is given to Colossae: “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry” (Col 3:5). The ground of the command is a crucifixion already accomplished: “they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts” (Gal 5:24). And again: “our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin” (Rom 6:6). Paul even uses the athlete's language of his own body: “I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection” (1Co 9:27). The verb is violent on purpose. Sin is not a weakness to be coached. It is a thing to be killed, and the Spirit is the one who makes the killing possible.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mortification, in Scripture, as the act of subduing the passions and appetites by penance, abstinence, or painful severities; and the mortification of the appetites and passions by self-denial as always a Christian duty.
webster_full: MORTIFICA'TION, n. [See Mortify.]
1. In medicine and surgery, the death and consequent putrefaction of one part of an animal body, while the rest is alive; gangrene.

2. In Scripture, the act of subduing the passions and appetites by penance, abstinence or painful severities inflicted on the body. The mortification of the appetites and passions by self-denial is always a christian duty.
3. Humiliation or slight vexation; the state of being humbled or depressed by disappointment.
Mortification is the local or partial death of a living animal body.
scriptures: Rom 8:13
For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live.
Col 3:5
Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry:
Gal 5:24
And they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts.
Rom 6:6
Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin.
But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.
corruption_summary: Mortification is replaced with self-improvement, or with a medieval punishing of the body that never touches the lusts Paul named.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic age will manage sin, name it as a pattern, and call the management growth. Romans 8:13 does not say manage. It says mortify, and it attaches a death to the refusal. The deeds of the body are not bad habits awaiting a better system. They are to be put to death through the Spirit. A congregation that talks much of authenticity and little of crucifixion has already traded Owen for a workshop.

The opposite error is the hair shirt. Webster recorded the old misuse: painful severities inflicted on the body as if the flesh Paul means were muscle and bone. Colossians 3:5 lists fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness. Those are not cured by hunger strikes. “Which is idolatry” gives the real target. The body may be kept under, as Paul kept his, but the killing is of the old man's loves, not of the creaturely body God made and will raise.

The order of the gospel must not be inverted. Galatians 5:24 says they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh. The indicative stands under the imperative. A man does not mortify in order to become Christ's. He mortifies because he is Christ's, and the Spirit who indwells him is not idle. Where there is no mortification at all, the claim to be in Romans 8 should be re-examined, not soothed.
roots_summary: Greek thanatoō (G2289), to put to death; nekroō (G3499), to make dead; stauroō (G4717), to crucify; Latin mortificare.
roots_lines: Greek thanatoō (G2289) — mortify; Romans 8:13, put the deeds of the body to death.
Greek nekroō (G3499) — mortify; Colossians 3:5, make dead the members on the earth.
Greek stauroō (G4717) — crucify; Galatians 5:24, the flesh with the affections and lusts.
usage: “If ye through the Spirit do mortify” — not through a system, and not optionally.
“Mortify therefore your members” — and the list is lusts, not muscle.
“Have crucified the flesh” — the killing is already begun in those who are Christ's.

pos: n. (the Spirit's work of opening the mind to understand, receive, and obey the already-given Word; not new revelation)
etymology: Latin illuminare, to light up, from lumen, light. In theology it names the Spirit's inward work with an outward Book. It is not a second Bible. It is eyesight for the one God has already spoken.
biblical_def: Illumination is the Holy Spirit's work of giving light so that a man can see what Scripture already says. The Book is not dark because God mumbled. The reader is dark because he is fallen. “But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned” (1Co 2:14). The psalmist therefore prays, “Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law” (Psa 119:18). Paul asks the same gift for the church: “that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give unto you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him” (Eph 1:17). The risen Christ did it in person on the road: “Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures” (Luk 24:45). And the saints have an anointing: “ye have an unction from the Holy One, and ye know all things” (1Jn 2:20). Illumination does not add verses. It makes the verses alive to a mind that would otherwise call them foolishness.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines illumination as the act of rendering luminous, and as infusion of intellectual light, an enlightening of the understanding by knowledge, or the mind by spiritual light; also inspiration, the special communication of knowledge to the mind by the Supreme Being.
webster_full: ILLUMINA'TION, n. The act of illuminating or rendering luminous; the act of supplying with light.
2. That which gives light. The sun is an illumination created.
3. Brightness; splendor.
4. Infusion of intellectual light; an enlightening of the understanding by knowledge, or the mind by spiritual light.
6. Inspiration; the special communication of knowledge to the mind by the Supreme Being.
scriptures: But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.
Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law.
Eph 1:17
That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give unto you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him:
Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures,
But ye have an unction from the Holy One, and ye know all things.
corruption_summary: Illumination is confused with new revelation, or denied altogether so that scholarship can replace the Spirit.
corruption_paragraphs: Charismatic misuse treats illumination as fresh speech on a par with Scripture: a word, an impression, a private disclosure that may sit beside the text or even overrule it. Luke 24:45 is the correction. He opened their understanding that they might understand the scriptures. The object is the Book already written. The Spirit who inspired it is not now writing a second one in the heart. He is making the first one seen.

The academic misuse is the reverse. 1 Corinthians 2:14 is treated as a relic of pre-critical piety. The natural man, given enough method, is said to be able to know the things of the Spirit of God after all. That is to make hermeneutics do the work of regeneration. Method is a due means. It is not a substitute for the unction from the Holy One. A man may parse John 3 and still call it foolishness until the Spirit gives him eyes.

Perspicuity and illumination are a pair, not rivals. The Word is clear; the reader is blind. God wrote plainly, and God must still open the eyes. Psalm 119:18 assumes both. The wondrous things are already in the law. The need is not a better law. It is opened eyes.
roots_summary: Greek phōtizō (G5461), to enlighten; dianoigō (G1272), to open; chrisma (G5545), unction; Hebrew galah (H1540), to uncover, of eyes.
roots_lines: Greek dianoigō (G1272) — to open; Luke 24:45, opened he their understanding.
Greek psychikos anthrōpos (G5591) — the natural man; 1 Corinthians 2:14, cannot know the things of the Spirit.
Greek chrisma (G5545) — unction, anointing; 1 John 2:20, 2:27, from the Holy One.
usage: “Neither can he know them” — the natural man, not the uneducated man.
“Open thou mine eyes” — the wondrous things are already in the law.
“Opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures” — the object is the Book, not a new one.

pos: n. (a pleading with God on behalf of another; Christ's unfinished priestly work, and the Spirit's inarticulate help, and the church's duty)
etymology: Latin intercessio, a going between, from intercedere (inter- between + cedere to go). The high priest went between God and the people with blood. Christ now goes between with His own.
biblical_def: Intercession is a going between: prayer or pleading offered to God for another. The church is commanded to it: “I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men” (1Ti 2:1). But the load-bearing Intercessor is not the church. It is the risen Christ: “Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them” (Heb 7:25). Paul locates that work at the Father's right hand: “who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us” (Rom 8:34). The Spirit does a different and inward work of the same name: “the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered” (Rom 8:26). And Isaiah had already put the vocation on the Servant: “he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors” (Isa 53:12). Christ's intercession is not a second sacrifice. It is the once-offered Priest presenting the finished work, always, for those who come unto God by Him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines intercession as the act of interceding; mediation; interposition between parties at variance, with a view to reconciliation; prayer or solicitation to one party in favor of another.
webster_full: INTERCES'SION, n. [L. intercessio, from intercedo. See Intercede.]
The act of interceding; mediation; interposition between parties at variance, with a view to reconciliation;
prayer or solicitation to one party in favor of another, sometimes against another.
He bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors. Isaiah 53:12.
scriptures: Heb 7:25
Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.
Rom 8:34
Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us.
Rom 8:26
Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.
I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men;

Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
corruption_summary: Christ's intercession is either forgotten, as if the cross were the whole priesthood, or farmed out to saints and a queen of heaven.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome installed a court of secondary intercessors — Mary, the saints, a priesthood that still mediates as if Hebrews were unfinished. Hebrews 7:25 gives the office to the One who ever liveth, and it gives the reason He can save to the uttermost: that living intercession. A dead saint cannot occupy it. A queen of heaven is a rival to it. The church on earth is commanded to make intercessions; it is never invited to share the unique priesthood of the Son.

Protestant forgetfulness is quieter. The cross is preached as finished, which it is, and then Christ is spoken of as if He were done working. Romans 8:34 will not have it. The same Christ who died, who is risen, who is at the right hand, also maketh intercession for us. The session is not retirement. A people that never thinks of Christ praying for them will soon pray as if everything depended on the heat of their own words.

The Spirit's groanings are not a second gospel. They are help in infirmity, because we know not what we should pray for as we ought. That is comfort for the inarticulate, not a license for uninterpreted utterance as a mark of standing. The Intercessor in heaven speaks clearly. The Spirit within translates our weakness. Neither replaces the Word.
roots_summary: Greek entygchanō (G1793), to fall in with, plead; enteuxis (G1783), intercession; Hebrew paga (H6293), to meet, make intercession.
roots_lines: Greek entygchanō (G1793) — to intercede; Hebrews 7:25, Romans 8:27, 8:34.
Greek enteuxis (G1783) — intercession; 1 Timothy 2:1, 4:5.
Hebrew paga (H6293) — to meet, lay upon, intercede; Isaiah 53:12, made intercession for the transgressors.
usage: “He ever liveth to make intercession” — the priesthood is not a past event.
“Who also maketh intercession for us” — said of the Christ who died and is risen.
“Intercessions... be made for all men” — the church's duty, not a rival priesthood.

pos: adj. (of the atonement: Christ suffered in the room and stead of His people, the just for the unjust)
etymology: Latin substituere, to put one in the place of another, from sub- under + statuere to set. The Bible's preposition is for — anti, hyper — a life given in the place of many.
biblical_def: Substitutionary names the heart of the atonement: Christ suffered in the place of sinners, bearing what was due to them, that they might receive what is due to Him. Isaiah said it before the word existed: “he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed” (Isa 53:5). Paul gives the exchange in one sentence: “For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (2Co 5:21). Peter makes the parties explicit: “Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God” (1Pe 3:18). The curse is not waived. It is borne: “Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us” (Gal 3:13). And the Son of man states His own errand: “to give his life a ransom for many” (Mar 10:45). This is not one theory on a shelf with moral influence and governmental display. Those may describe fruits. They do not explain the wounds.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines substitution as the act of putting one person or thing in the place of another to supply its place; as the substitution of an agent, attorney or representative to act for one in his absence.
webster_full: SUBSTITU'TION, n. The act of putting one person or thing in the place of another to supply its place;
as the substitution of an agent, attorney or representative to act for one in his absence;
the substitution of bank notes for gold and silver, as a circulating medium.
1. In grammar, syllepsis, or the use of one word for another.
scriptures: Isa 53:5
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.
For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit:
Gal 3:13
Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree:
For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.
corruption_summary: The wounds are turned into an example of love, or a display to the universe, anything except a penalty borne in another man's room.
corruption_paragraphs: Moral-influence readings keep the love and empty the justice. Christ dies to show how much God cares, and the sinner is moved to repent. Isaiah 53 will not go into that mold. The chastisement of our peace was upon him. Wounded for our transgressions is not wounded to inspire us. A display that does not bear anything leaves the guilt where it was.

Governmental and exemplary theories do the same work with more dignity. God must show that He hates sin, so He makes a public example of His Son. Peter says the just suffered for the unjust, that He might bring us to God. The preposition is substitution, not theatre. And Galatians 3:13 is still more stubborn: He was made a curse for us. An example is not made a curse. A substitute is.

The ransom word is particular. A ransom for many, not a potential payment left on the table for whoever will pick it up. The dictionary's standard is definite atonement: the work effectually for the elect. Universalizing the substitution until it substitutes for no one in particular is how the doctrine is kept as a slogan and lost as a gospel.
roots_summary: Greek anti (G473), in place of; hyper (G5228), on behalf of; lytron (G3083), ransom; Hebrew chalal (H2490), to wound; the Servant songs' for.
roots_lines: Greek lytron anti pollōn (G3083, G473) — a ransom for many; Mark 10:45, Matthew 20:28.
Greek hyper hēmōn hamartia (G5228) — sin for us; 2 Corinthians 5:21.
Hebrew mecholal mipeshaenu — wounded for our transgressions; Isaiah 53:5, the for that carries the gospel.
usage: “The just for the unjust” — the parties are named, and the direction is one way.
“Made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin” — the exchange, not a demonstration.
“A ransom for many” — paid, not merely priced.

pos: n. (the body; mankind; and, in Paul, the old corrupt nature that lusts against the Spirit)
etymology: Hebrew basar (H1320), flesh, kin, all living. Greek sarx (G4561), flesh. One English word has to carry the body God made, the Word made flesh, and the principle that cannot please God. The context decides, and it must be allowed to.
biblical_def: Flesh in Scripture is not one thing, and the sermon that treats it as one thing will curse the body or spare the sin. First, the Word took it: “And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). That flesh is creaturely humanity, without sin. Second, flesh is the old principle in man that will not submit. “So then they that are in the flesh cannot please God” (Rom 8:8). Third, it is the present conflict of the Christian: “For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would” (Gal 5:17). Paul will not flatter the remaining corruption: “For I know that in me (that is, in my flesh,) dwelleth no good thing” (Rom 7:18). And those who are Christ's have a crucifixion to match it: “they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts” (Gal 5:24). The body is not the enemy. The flesh-as-principle is. Confusing them produces either Gnostic hatred of the creature or a polite Christianity that never mortifies.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines flesh as the body distinguished from the soul; human nature; carnality; a carnal state, a state of unrenewed nature; and notes that they that are in the flesh cannot please God.
webster_full: FLESH, n. A compound substance forming a large part of an animal, consisting of the softer solids, as distinguished from the bones and the fluids.
4. The body, as distinguished from the soul.
7. Human nature. The word was made flesh and dwelt among us. John 1.
8. Carnality; corporeal appetites. The flesh lusteth against the spirit. Galatians 5:17.
9. A carnal state; a state of unrenewed nature. They that are in the flesh cannot please God. Romans 8:8.
scriptures: John 1:14
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
Rom 8:8
So then they that are in the flesh cannot please God.
Gal 5:17
For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would.
Rom 7:18
For I know that in me (that is, in my flesh,) dwelleth no good thing: for to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not.
Gal 5:24
And they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts.
corruption_summary: The body is either treated as the problem, or Paul's flesh is reduced to 'embodied life' so that nothing in us needs crucifying.
corruption_paragraphs: Gnostic and some ascetic readings hear sarx and start punishing the creature. John 1:14 forbids it. The Word was made flesh. God the Son took a true body, and He will raise ours. Fasting may keep the body under. Hatred of the body is another religion.

The modern reverse is more common in pulpits that want to sound kind. Flesh is restated as our embodied, situated, human condition — something to be honored, not crucified. Then Galatians 5:24 becomes an embarrassment. Paul crucified affections and lusts, not a skeleton. Romans 8:8 is not about people who happen to have bodies. It is about those still located in the old principle, who cannot please God. A Christianity that cannot say that sentence will not mortify, and will not understand why the Spirit's opposition feels like war.

Romans 7:18 must be read as a believer's confession, not as a license. No good thing dwells in the flesh, and yet the man who says so is the man who delights in the law of God after the inward man. The conflict is the evidence of two principles, not the proof that regeneration has failed. Galatians 5:17 says the same to people walking in the Spirit. The flesh is not gone. It is opposed. That is the Christian life until glory.
roots_summary: Hebrew basar (H1320), flesh, kin; Greek sarx (G4561), flesh; sarkikos (G4559), fleshly; epithumeō (G1937), to lust.
roots_lines: Hebrew basar (H1320) — flesh, mankind, kin; Genesis 6:3, 2:24, Isaiah 40:5.
Greek sarx (G4561) — flesh; John 1:14, Romans 8:8, Galatians 5:17, 5:24.
Greek sarkikos (G4559) — fleshly, carnal; Romans 7:14, 1 Corinthians 3:1.
usage: “The Word was made flesh” — so the body is not the enemy.
“They that are in the flesh cannot please God” — location, not anatomy.
“The flesh lusteth against the Spirit” — written to people who have the Spirit.

pos: n. (hearing that does what is commanded; the Son's obedience unto death, and the believer's fruit of faith)
etymology: Latin obedientia, from obedire, to hearken, to submit to a hearing. Hebrew shama (H8085) is to hear, and so to obey. In Scripture a man has not heard if he has not done.
biblical_def: Obedience is not the same as being agreeable. It is doing what God has said because He has said it. Samuel put the knife to ritual religion: “Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams” (1Sa 15:22). The Son's own path is named with the same word: “he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Php 2:8). Hebrews adds that “though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered” (Heb 5:8). That is active obedience as well as the suffering of death, and it is the righteousness imputed to those who are in Him. The believer's obedience is then a yielding: “to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are to whom ye obey; whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness” (Rom 6:16). And it has a means: “Seeing ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit” (1Pe 1:22). Faith is not the opposite of obedience. It is the root. Obedience is the fruit. A faith that will not obey is not the faith of Abraham, and it is not the faith that justifies.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines obedience as compliance with a command, prohibition, or known law; and insists that voluntary obedience alone can be acceptable to God, and that obedience is not synonymous with obsequiousness.
webster_full: OBE'DIENCE, n. [L. obedientia. See Obey.]

Compliance with a command, prohibition or known law and rule of duty prescribed; the performance of what is required or enjoined by authority, or the abstaining from what is prohibited, in compliance with the command or prohibition.

To constitute obedience the act or forbearance to act must be in submission to authority; the command must be known to the person, and his compliance must be in consequence of it, or it is not obedience.
Obedience is not synonymous with obsequiousness; the latter often implying meanness or servility, and obedience being merely a proper submission to authority.
Voluntary obedience alone can be acceptable to God.
scriptures: And Samuel said, Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.
Php 2:8
And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
Heb 5:8
Though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered;
Rom 6:16
Know ye not, that to whom ye yield yourselves servants to obey, his servants ye are to whom ye obey; whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness?
Seeing ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit unto unfeigned love of the brethren, see that ye love one another with a pure heart fervently:
corruption_summary: Obedience is treated as the enemy of grace, or as the whole of the gospel, and both errors refuse the Son's obedience in the sinner's place.
corruption_paragraphs: Cheap grace hears “not of works” and then treats obedience as a threat to assurance. Romans 6:16 will not permit a third category, a Christian who yields to no one. You are servant to whom you obey. If the truth has been obeyed through the Spirit, the soul is purified unto love of the brethren. A profession that will not hearken is the sacrifice Samuel rejected: religion offered instead of the thing commanded.

Legalism makes the opposite exchange. Obedience becomes the ground of acceptance, and Christ's “obedient unto death” is reduced to an example to copy rather than a righteousness to receive. The dictionary's standard is the active obedience of Christ imputed, as well as His death. Hebrews 5:8 is about the Son learning obedience in His humiliation, not about you climbing into His office. Your obedience is fruit. His is the title.

1 Samuel 15:22 also judges the evangelical instinct to substitute a better technique for the thing God actually said. Saul had reasons. He had cattle for sacrifice. He had a story. Samuel called it rebellion. Hearing that does not do is not hearing. That is as true of the regulative principle in worship as it is of the moral law in the life.
roots_summary: Hebrew shama (H8085), to hear, obey; Greek hypakoē (G5218), obedience; hypēkoos (G5255), obedient; hypakouō (G5219), to hearken.
roots_lines: Hebrew shama (H8085) — to hear, so to obey; 1 Samuel 15:22, Deuteronomy 6:4, Exodus 19:5.
Greek hypakoē (G5218) — obedience; Romans 6:16, Hebrews 5:8, 1 Peter 1:2.
Greek hypēkoos (G5255) — obedient; Philippians 2:8, obedient unto death.
usage: “To obey is better than sacrifice” — said to a king who had a religious reason.
“Obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” — the title, not merely the example.
“His servants ye are to whom ye obey” — there is no third master.

pos: n. (the creational order: male and female equal in the image, distinct in office; headship in the house and male eldership in the church)
etymology: From complement, that which completes, not compliment. The -arian label is late, a twentieth-century name for what Genesis 1-2 and the household texts already taught. The thing is as old as the rib.
biblical_def: Complementarianism is the creational teaching that man and woman are equal in dignity as image-bearers and distinct in the offices God assigned. Equality is not in dispute: “So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them” (Gen 1:27). Distinction is not a bruise of the Fall. It is given before the Fall: “It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him” (Gen 2:18). Paul traces headship to that order, not to local custom: “the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church” (Eph 5:23). The household command is equally plain: “Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as unto the Lord” (Eph 5:22). And the church's office is bounded with the same grain: “I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence” (1Ti 2:12). The archetype is not Roman household codes. It is this: “the head of every man is Christ; and the head of the woman is the man; and the head of Christ is God” (1Co 11:3). Headship in the house is patterned on Christ. Male eldership in the church is the same grain run through 1 Timothy 3. The woman's glory is not a lesser image. It is a different office.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines complement as fullness, completion, whence perfection; and as full quantity or number. The theological name is later; the creational fact is that the woman is given as the help meet who completes the man, not as a duplicate of him.
webster_full: COMPLEMENT, n. Fulness; completion; whence, perfection.
2. Full quantity or number; the quantity or number limited; as, a company has its complement of men.
3. That which is added, not as necessary, but as ornamental; something adventitious to the main thing; ceremony.
The word in theology is not Webster's -ism. It names the older fact: the sexes complete one another under a head, they do not compete as interchangeable units.
scriptures: Gen 1:27
So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
Gen 2:18
And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.
Eph 5:23
For the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church: and he is the saviour of the body.
Eph 5:22
Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as unto the Lord.
But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence.
corruption_summary: Equality of image is used to erase distinction of office, and headship is renamed oppression so that the church can copy the world's interchangeable sexes.
corruption_paragraphs: Egalitarianism keeps Genesis 1:27 and then files off Genesis 2:18. Male and female become two instances of the same office, and every text that assigns headship is re-read as a local brake on a first-century abuse. Paul will not allow the move. He grounds 1 Timothy 2 in creation and the Fall, not in Ephesus, and he names the husband's headship as the copy of Christ's. If that headship is oppression, then Christ is the oppressor of the church. The argument proves too much, and that is how you know it is wrong.

The other corruption is the harshness that forgets the other half of Ephesians 5. Headship that will not give itself up, that will not nourish and cherish, is not complementarian. It is the old tyranny the gospel came to kill. The husband is the head even as Christ is the head of the church, and He is the Saviour of the body. A man who cites 1 Timothy 2:12 and will not wash feet has not understood the office he is so eager to keep.

Modern sex-revolt goes further than evangelical egalitarianism. It detaches “identity” from the body God created male and female. The dictionary names that as a corruption of Genesis 1:27, not as a pastoral puzzle with two legitimate sides. The image is sexed. The offices are sexed. The gospel does not flatten the sexes. It restores them to their created grain, in the house and in the church.
roots_summary: Hebrew zakar / neqebah (H2145, H5347), male and female; ezer kenegdo, a help corresponding to him; Greek kephalē (G2776), head; hypotassō (G5293), to submit.
roots_lines: Hebrew ezer kenegdo (H5828, H5048) — a help meet, corresponding to him; Genesis 2:18, 2:20.
Greek kephalē (G2776) — head; Ephesians 5:23, 1 Corinthians 11:3, Colossians 1:18.
Greek authenteō (G831) — to usurp authority; 1 Timothy 2:12, the verb Paul will not permit a woman over a man in the church's teaching office.
usage: “Male and female created he them” — two sexes, one image, no third kind.
“An help meet for him” — corresponding, not interchangeable.
“The husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ” — the pattern, not a metaphor you can drop.

pos: n. phrase (the Arminian claim that grace goes before in all men to restore ability to believe; not the Bible's effectual call)
etymology: Latin praevenire, to come before, to anticipate. Webster knew the adjective: going before; hence, preventive; as prevenient grace. The thing Arminians mean by it is a universal restoration of ability. The thing Scripture means by grace that goes before is the Father drawing particular men.
biblical_def: Prevenient grace, in the Arminian use, is a gracious work said to go before conversion in all men, sufficiently undoing the inability of the Fall so that every sinner can believe if he will. The motive is to keep a universal gospel offer and a fallen race at once. The texts will not carry it. Christ does not say that all men, once assisted, may come. He says, “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day” (John 6:44). He repeats the bar: “no man can come unto me, except it were given unto him of my Father” (John 6:65). The natural condition is not weakness. It is death: “And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins” (Eph 2:1). The same sentence locates the life-giving in God, not in a restored will: “Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;)” (Eph 2:5). And the carnal mind “is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be” (Rom 8:7). Grace does go before. It goes before as the Father's drawing and the Spirit's quickening of the elect, not as a flashlight handed to every corpse.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prevenient as going before; preceding; hence, preventive; as prevenient grace. The adjective is honest. The Arminian universalising of it is not.
webster_full: PREVE'NIENT, a. [L. preveniens.] Going before; preceding;
hence, preventive; as prevenient grace.
The word in Webster is the adjective. It does not decide whether the grace that goes before is particular or universal.
The Confession's word for the saving work that goes before faith is effectual calling, not a restored ability in all mankind.
scriptures: John 6:44
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.
John 6:65
And he said, Therefore said I unto you, that no man can come unto me, except it were given unto him of my Father.
Eph 2:1
And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins;
Eph 2:5
Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;)
Rom 8:7
Because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be.
corruption_summary: A grace that goes before is a biblical thought. Making it a universal repair of the will is how Arminianism keeps the language of grace and the reality of self-election.
corruption_paragraphs: Give the Arminian his concern. If men are dead, and if Christ is preached to all, how is the offer sincere? The Reformed answer is not a repaired will in every hearer. It is a well-meant outward call, and an inward call that actually raises the dead. John 6:44 binds drawing to raising: the one drawn is the one raised at the last day. A drawing that can fail is not the drawing Jesus named.

Prevenient grace as a system puts the decisive moment back in the sinner. God has done His part; now you do yours. That is synergism with a polite prefix. Ephesians 2:5 will not have the corpse cooperating. He quickened us when we were dead. By grace ye are saved. The grace that goes before in that text is the quickening itself, not a prior gift of possible faith distributed to the race.

Romans 8:7 closes the loophole. The carnal mind is not subject, neither indeed can be. A universal prevenient grace that makes the mind able to subject itself has already rewritten the verse. What Scripture calls grace is stronger than that, and narrower: it actually saves. The dictionary's word for it is the effectual call. Keep the adjective prevenient for what comes first. Do not let it smuggle in a will that can still say no to the God who raises the dead.
roots_summary: Latin praevenire, to come before; Greek helkō (G1670), to draw; nekros (G3498), dead; zōopoieō (G2227), to quicken.
roots_lines: Greek helkō (G1670) — to draw; John 6:44, 12:32. In 6:44 the drawn are the raised.
Greek nekros (G3498) — dead; Ephesians 2:1, 2:5, Colossians 2:13 — the state grace finds, not a weakened ability.
Greek zōopoieō (G2227) — to quicken; Ephesians 2:5, Romans 8:11, the verb prevenient-grace-as-system will not let God monopolize.
usage: “No man can come to me, except the Father... draw him” — and the drawn are raised.
“Dead in trespasses and sins” — not impaired. Dead.
“Neither indeed can be” — the carnal mind, after whatever universal assist men imagine.
